html:
Requirements are the contract between the business and the build team — the only artifact both sides agree to be bound by. This phase teaches you to write functional and non-functional requirements, structure them in a Business Requirements Document (BRD), prioritize them with MoSCoW and value/effort, and keep every requirement traceable to a source, a story, and a test. Requirements Elicitation is 18% of the CBA exam, and this phase is its home.

Learning Objectives

  • Write clear functional and non-functional requirements...
  • Structure a Business Requirements Document with numbered sections...
  • Prioritize with MoSCoW and value/effort scoring...
  • Keep every requirement traceable to a source, a story, and a test case...
  • Write requirements that are testable and unambiguous...
  • Review requirements for hidden assumptions and double meanings...
  • Route requirements through the approval process in the lab...
  • Use Business_Requirement__c and RequirementsTraceabilityService in practice...

1. Requirements: The Contract Between Business and Build

A requirement is a statement of what the system must do, precise enough that a developer can build it and a tester can verify it. It is not a wish, a slide, or a meeting note: it is the durable artifact the business approves, the team builds, and UAT later proves. "Route leads faster" is a slogan; "every inbound web lead must be assigned a dispatcher owner within 60 seconds of submission" is a requirement.

The disciplines of this phase exist because a requirement fixed during Discovery costs almost nothing, and the same requirement fixed during UAT costs a sprint. The three enemies of good requirements are vagueness ("as soon as possible"), hidden ambiguity ("when the opportunity closes, notify the manager" — which manager?), and untestability. Everything here is a weapon against those three.

2. Functional Requirements: What the System Does

Functional requirements state WHAT the system does — the features, behavior, and capabilities. They are typically testable by performing an action and observing the result. BrightLogistics examples: "the system must create a Call task when a Lead status changes to Qualified," "the system must suppress duplicate Leads that share email and company," "the system must route high-priority cases to tier-1."

Write each functional requirement as an active sentence with a subject that can do the action. Use the imperative or "must" form, name the object and the field involved, and include the trigger condition. "The system must assign the Lead to the dispatcher with the fewest open assignments when the Lead status is Submitted" beats "leads should be distributed fairly" on every axis — object, rule, trigger, and measurable outcome are all present.

3. Non-Functional Requirements: How Well the System Performs

Non-functional requirements state HOW WELL the system performs — speed, security, usability, availability, compliance. They are easy to skip and expensive to skip: a dashboard meeting every functional need but taking three minutes to load has failed its users. They qualify the functional set, and on the exam they hide in questions like "the Case list view must support 50,000 records" — a volume and performance statement, not a feature.

TypeFocusExample
FunctionalFeatures and behaviorAuto-create a Task when an Opportunity reaches Closed Won
Non-functionalQuality attributesDashboard loads in under 3 seconds for 1M records
DataInformation rulesDuplicate leads suppressed by email + company
ReportingInsight needsExecutives can see pipeline conversion by source

For BrightLogistics the non-functional set is short and tied to the KPI: the routing decision must complete in under 5 seconds, the web form must accept 50 concurrent submissions without data loss, and dispatchers on a 4G connection in the yard must still load today's queue.

4. Data and Reporting Requirements

Data requirements describe the information rules the system must enforce: what is captured, how it is validated, how it is protected, how duplicates are handled. "Inbound web leads must be deduplicated on email and company name" is a data requirement; "the lead's original source must never be overwritten after assignment" is another. Reporting requirements describe the insight needs: who sees what, at what granularity, how often. "Dispatchers must see a real-time queue of unassigned leads sorted by submission time" is a reporting requirement.

Data and reporting requirements matter to the data model of Phase 5. A reporting requirement that needs dispatch cycle time forces the data model to store a dispatch timestamp; a data requirement that forbids empty carrier fields forces a validation rule. In the BRD these two types get their own section so the build team knows to read them before finalizing fields and report types.

5. Writing Testable Requirements

Use the "Invest" test as a quality gate: each requirement must be Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, and Testable. The most neglected letter is Testable. Before writing any requirement, ask: can I write a pass/fail check? "Usable interface" fails; "a dispatcher with the Business_Analyst permission set can assign a Lead in two clicks" passes — a tester scripts those two clicks and records the outcome.

Testability is also the fix for the three enemies. Vagueness dies to numbers ("under 3 seconds," "60 seconds," "two clicks"). Ambiguity dies to named objects and named rules. Untestability dies to the pass/fail question itself. A requirement you cannot verify is a wish — if you cannot write a pass/fail check, rewrite it until you can. This discipline carries directly into Phase 12, where each UAT test case descends from a testable requirement.

6. The Business Requirements Document (BRD) Structure

The BRD is the container that makes requirements reviewable. Follow the canonical seven-part structure so every stakeholder knows where to look:

  1. Background and business goals — why now, and the KPI.
  2. Scope — in scope and out of scope, stated explicitly.
  3. Stakeholders and roles — a RACI summary from Phase 2.
  4. As-is and to-be process summaries — from the Phase 3 maps.
  5. Functional requirements — numbered, testable, one per line.
  6. Non-functional, data, and reporting requirements — the qualified set.
  7. Assumptions, dependencies, and open questions — what is believed, what blocks, what is unknown.

For BrightLogistics, section 2 is where the discipline shows: "out of scope — customer-facing tracking portal at go-live" stops the portal wish from leaking into the lead-routing build. Section 4 carries the two swimlane thumbnails so readers see the before and after. Sections 5 and 6 are the meat; the rest is context that makes them interpretable.

7. Numbering and Wording Rules

Number every requirement (R-101, R-102, R-103...) so teams can trace and test them. The number is a permanent id: it survives rewording, appears on the user story that implements the requirement, and is cited in the UAT test case that proves it. Renamed requirements keep their number; deleted requirements go to a retired appendix, never disappear.

Wording rules keep the numbers meaningful. One requirement per sentence — an "and" that hides two needs becomes two numbers. Use must / should / shall consistently, RFC-2119 style: "must" is mandatory, "should" is a strong preference, "shall" appears only where the spec demands a guaranteed behavior. If a reviewer asks "is this mandatory?", the wording already answered. The Business_Requirement__c object's Requirement_Type__c and Priority__c fields let the lab enforce part of this as data.

8. Reviewing Requirements for Ambiguity

A review is a hunt for the sentence that two honest readers interpret differently. Read every requirement aloud: does the developer know exactly what to build, and does the tester know exactly what to check? Watch for pronouns without antecedents ("notify the manager and confirm they received it" — who?), qualified adjectives ("a reasonable number of fields"), and temporal sloppiness ("immediately" — in what hours?).

Peer review changes minds gently: each reviewer reads the BRD for only their own stake. The developer scans for buildability and gaps. The tester scans for testability. The business owner scans for scope creep hidden in wording. The three readers catch ninety percent of ambiguity before the requirement ever reaches the approval process. The acceptance criteria field on Business_Requirement__c (Acceptance_Criteria__c) is where the review's conclusion is parked: the pass/fail check itself, which is required before a requirement may be approved.

9. Prioritization with MoSCoW

MoSCoW sorts scope for a release: Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have. Must means the release fails without it — for BrightLogistics, web-to-lead capture, auto-assignment, and the dispatcher queue. Should means important and pursued, but negotiable if time runs out. Could means nice to have, the first place to cut. Won't means explicitly excluded this release — recorded on purpose, so nobody reopens the fight.

The value of "Won't Have" is underrated. A request that lands in Won't Have with a recorded reason is scope that stopped being a threat. The customer portal is BrightLogistics' classic Won't Have for release one: Greg wants it, but it does not serve the entry KPI, and everyone agrees to defer it in writing. MoSCoW converts the emotion of "we need everything" into a ranked table the whole release plan cites.

10. Value/Effort and the Priority Score

MoSCoW sorts by business value; value/effort pairs value with cost. Plot each requirement on a two-axis grid: value to the business (did we serve the KPI?) against effort to deliver (platform-native is cheap; integration is not). The winners are high-value, low-effort — capture them early. High-value, high-effort items get sequenced deliberately, not dropped. Low-value items, whatever the effort, get challenged: delete, defer, or demote to Could Have.

The lab computes a priority score to keep the ranking honest. Value_Score__c (1-100) and Gap_Score__c on Business_Requirement__c feed BacklogPrioritizationService, which yields one sortable number: a route-high-priority-cases requirement at value 95 outranks a reporting nicety at 40, mechanically. Exercise 4.2 MoSCoW prioritization in Phase 15 runs a full release ranking.

11. Traceability: Requirement to Story to Test Case

Traceability links three artifacts: each requirement to the user story that implements it, and each story to the UAT test case that proves it. The goal is full coverage: every requirement covered by at least one story, and every story by at least one UAT test case. Coverage is computed as tested divided by total, and gaps are exposed as red flags in Phase 11's traceability report.

apex
// RequirementsTraceabilityService keeps Requirement -> Story -> Test links
Business_Requirement__c r = new Business_Requirement__c(
  Name                = 'Route high-priority cases to tier 1',
  Requirement_Type__c = 'Functional',
  Priority__c         = 'Must Have',
  Status__c           = 'In Review'   // awaiting approval flow
);

Traceability is how you answer the two questions every project eventually asks. "Did we build everything we promised?" is answered by looking for requirements with no stories. "Did we prove what we built?" is answered by looking for stories with no test cases. The RequirementsTraceabilityService in force-app/main/default/classes/RequirementsTraceabilityService.cls computes both sides, and a story with no test case is a coverage gap the BA cannot allow into sign-off.

12. The Requirement Approval Process in the Lab

A requirement becomes binding the moment it is approved. The lab models that gate with the Requirement_Approval_Routing Flow (force-app/main/default/flows/Requirement_Approval_Routing.flow-meta.xml) and the approval process Business_Requirement__c.Requirements_Approval (force-app/main/default/approvalProcesses/). The flow submits the record when Status__c becomes Submitted; the process routes it to a single approver; the decision is recorded; and the platform event Requirement_Status_Changed__e notifies subscribers like the approval dashboard.

Study the flow's decision logic: it refuses to submit Draft requirements (no approval of a wish), routes by Requirement_Type__c (functional to the solution architect, reporting to the report owner), and parks In Review requirements until Acceptance_Criteria__c is present. The gate enforces everything earlier in this phase — you cannot approve what is not numbered, testable, and complete.

13. Assumptions, Dependencies, and Open Questions

Every BRD ends with the truth about what is not yet known. Assumptions are beliefs the plan depends on — "the web form vendor can add a webhook by go-live." Dependencies are things outside the project that must happen — "the email domain migration completes in week 2." Open questions are logged, owned, and dated — "who owns the first call: sales or dispatch?" — each with a name and a next resolution date.

Used correctly, this section makes the BRD honest instead of hopeful. An assumption that turns out false is a change request with a paper trail, not a surprise. An open question with a named owner is a problem being worked; an open question with no owner is a risk. Phase 6 picks up the open questions as user story context, and Phase 13's change management uses the assumptions log as the starting list of things that might move — the traceability discipline extends to the document's own uncertainty.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 4.1: Write Requirements From the To-Be Process

  1. Take the BrightLogistics to-be swimlane from the Phase 3 exercises.
  2. Write one functional requirement per to-be step, one non-functional requirement for the routing speed, one data requirement (dedupe rule), and one reporting requirement (queue dashboard).
  3. Number each requirement R-101 upward and apply a pass/fail check to every one.
  4. Harsh test: rewrite any requirement that fails the pass/fail question.

Expected result: a numbered requirement set (at least six) where every line passes the testability check. What it proves: process change converts directly into testable requirements. This pairs with Exercise 4.1 Requirement writing from the to-be process in Phase 15.

Exercise 4.2: MoSCoW and Value/Effort Ranking Workshop

  1. Take the set from Exercise 4.1 plus three extras: customer portal, SMS dispatcher alerts, offline queue sync.
  2. Sort all of them into Must, Should, Could, Won't for the first release.
  3. Score each Must/Should on Value_Score__c (1-100) and Gap_Score__c, and sort the list by the resulting priority.
  4. Justify one demotion and one Won't Have in writing.

Expected result: a MoSCoW table with a justified rank, at least one explicit Won't Have, and a defensible priority order. What it proves: you can make scope decisions that survive review. Pairs with Exercise 4.2 MoSCoW prioritization in Phase 15.

Exercise 4.3: Build the Traceability Matrix

  1. Create the requirement records from Exercise 4.1 in the org with Status__c Approved.
  2. Create (or stub) one user story per requirement and one UAT test case per story.
  3. Run the traceability check: requirements without stories, stories without test cases.
  4. Report the coverage percentage and list the gaps.

Expected result: a traceability matrix you can compute coverage from, with named gaps, matching the red-flag report in Phase 11. What it proves: traceability is a data query, not a sentiment. Pairs with Exercise 4.3 Traceability matrix in Phase 15.

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
RequirementA precise statement of what the system must do, buildable and verifiable.
Functional requirementWhat the system does: features, behavior, capabilities.
Non-functional requirementHow well the system performs: speed, security, volume, availability.
BRDBusiness Requirements Document, the container that makes requirements reviewable.
RFC-2119 wordingDisciplined use of must, should, and shall to remove ambiguity.
Invest testRequirement quality gate: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
MoSCoWScope sorting: Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, Won't Have.
Value/effortTwo-axis prioritization pairing business value with delivery cost.
Value_Score__c1-100 business-value input on Business_Requirement__c used in priority scoring.
TraceabilityThe Requirement to Story to Test Case link that proves coverage.
Coverage gapA requirement without a story, or a story without a test case.
Assumptions logDocumented beliefs and open questions, each owned and dated.

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can write a functional and a non-functional requirement from the same to-be step.
  • I can structure a BRD with the seven canonical sections.
  • I can apply the pass/fail testability check to any requirement.
  • I can prioritize a release with MoSCoW and justify the Won't Haves.
  • I can compute value/effort and the priority score for a backlog.
  • I can build a Requirement to Story to Test Case traceability matrix and report coverage.
  • I can number and word requirements RFC-2119 style with one requirement per line.
  • I can route a requirement through the approval flow and explain why the gate exists.

Summary

You learned to write functional, non-functional, data, and reporting requirements, and to containerize them in a seven-part BRD every stakeholder can navigate. You applied the Invest test and RFC-2119 wording to make each requirement testable and unambiguous. You ranked requirements with MoSCoW and value/effort, kept them traceable through the Requirement to Story to Test Case chain, and enforced the whole discipline with the approval process in the lab. The numbered, approved requirements you produce here are exactly the raw material Phase 6 turns into user stories and Phase 12 turns into UAT test cases.
